nodes.label: Diocletian (abdication)
nodes.full: Diocletian abdicates voluntarily on 1 May 305 — the only emperor in this era to retire peacefully; his palace at Split still inhabited today.
nodes.src: Abdication date: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 19. Palace at Split (Spalatum): extant, UNESCO. Lactantius and Eutropius 9.26 both record the abdication.

nodes.label: Galerius
nodes.full: Eastern Augustus after Diocletian's abdication; issued the Edict of Toleration (311) on his deathbed, ending the Great Persecution.
nodes.src: Edict of Toleration 311: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 33–34 (full text). Eusebius HE 8.17. Died May 311 — both sources agree.

nodes.label: Maxentius
nodes.full: Son of Maximian who seized power in Rome against the Tetrarchic system; controlled Italy and Africa until defeated and drowned at the Milvian Bridge.
nodes.src: SHA Vita Maxentii (disputed authenticity). Defeated at Milvian Bridge 28 Oct 312 — Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 44; Eusebius Vita Const. 1.37–38.

nodes.label: Constantine I ('the Great')
nodes.full: Reunified the empire, legalised Christianity, founded Constantinople, convened Nicaea — the most consequential emperor since Augustus.
nodes.src: Victory at Milvian Bridge 28 Oct 312: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 44; Eusebius VC 1.28–29. Death 22 May 337 at Nicomedia — Eusebius VC 4.62. Extensive coinage throughout reign.

nodes.label: Licinius
nodes.full: Constantine's co-emperor and brother-in-law who co-signed the Edict of Milan (313); defeated and executed by Constantine in 324.
nodes.src: Edict of Milan 313: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 48 (full Latin text). Defeated at Chrysopolis 18 Sep 324 — Zosimus 2.25; Eusebius VC 2.15–18.

nodes.label: Constantius II
nodes.full: Sole emperor from 353; devoted Arian Christian who expelled the pro-Nicene bishop Athanasius five times and tried to impose Arian Christianity empire-wide.
nodes.src: Athanasius's own letters document the five exiles. Ammianus Marcellinus 21.16 records Constantius's death 3 Nov 361 at Mopsucrene. Extensive Arian synod records survive.

nodes.label: Julian ('the Apostate')
nodes.full: Constantine's nephew who publicly renounced Christianity and attempted to restore traditional Roman religion; died on the Persian campaign he himself launched.
nodes.src: Julian's own writings survive: Orations, Letters, Against the Galileans (fragments). Died 26 Jun 363 near Samarra — Ammianus Marcellinus 25.3. Libanius Oratio 18 (funeral oration).

nodes.label: Jovian
nodes.full: Christian general elected by the army on Julian's death; concluded the humiliating peace with Persia ceding Nisibis, then died after 8 months.
nodes.src: Peace of 363: Ammianus Marcellinus 25.7 records terms. Death at Dadastana: Ammianus 25.10. Eutropius 10.17 confirms date. Nisibis cession documented in multiple sources.

nodes.label: Valentinian I (West)
nodes.full: Capable military emperor who spent his reign fortifying the Rhine frontier; died of a stroke while angrily haranguing a Gothic delegation.
nodes.src: Death 17 Nov 375 at Brigetio — Ammianus Marcellinus 30.6. Rhine fortification programme: Ammianus 28.2. Zosimus 4.17. Multiple inscription evidence from Rhine forts.

nodes.label: Valens (East)
nodes.full: Eastern emperor who admitted the Goths across the Danube in 376 and was killed at the Battle of Adrianople — his body never found.
nodes.src: Death at Adrianople 9 Aug 378 — Ammianus Marcellinus 31.13. Zosimus 4.24. Eunapius fragments. Body never recovered: Ammianus 31.13.15.

nodes.label: Gratian (West)
nodes.full: Young Western emperor who removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate and stripped pagan priests of their stipends; murdered in a military revolt.
nodes.src: Altar of Victory dispute: Symmachus Relatio 3 (384) and Ambrose Epistulae 17–18 (both survive in full). Murdered Lugdunum 25 Aug 383 — Zosimus 4.35.

nodes.label: Theodosius I (East, then sole)
nodes.full: Made Christianity the only legal religion of the empire (380 & 391); baptised on his deathbed in 380, then became sole emperor — the last to rule a united empire.
nodes.src: Edict of Thessalonica 27 Feb 380: Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 (full text survives). Sole emperor from 394. Death 17 Jan 395 at Milan — Zosimus 4.59; Claudian's panegyric.

nodes.label: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
nodes.full: Constantine defeats Maxentius, who drowns in the Tiber — the battle after which Constantine attributes his victory to the Christian god.
nodes.src: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 44 (chi-rho dream). Eusebius VC 1.28–29 (cross in sky). Panegyrici Latini 12 (313) — contemporary oration. Bridge and site identified.

nodes.label: Battle of Chrysopolis
nodes.full: Constantine defeats Licinius to become sole emperor of the reunified Roman world — the last civil war until the 350s.
nodes.src: Zosimus 2.25. Eusebius VC 2.15–18. Anonymus Valesianus 5.27–28. Licinius subsequently executed — Zosimus 2.28.

nodes.label: Julian's Persian campaign
nodes.full: Julian leads a massive invasion of Persia, reaches Ctesiphon but cannot take it, then is mortally wounded during the retreat — ending the campaign in disaster.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 23–25 (detailed eyewitness account). Julian's own letters document preparations. Death 26 Jun 363: Ammianus 25.3. Zosimus 3.12–29.

nodes.label: Peace of 363 — cession of Nisibis
nodes.full: Rome cedes Nisibis and 15 frontier towns to Persia — the most humiliating territorial concession in Roman history, forced after Julian's disastrous campaign.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 25.7 records full terms. Ephrem the Syrian's Carmina Nisibena (Syriac poems) document the Roman evacuation — primary eyewitness.

nodes.label: Gothic crossing of the Danube
nodes.full: Valens admits around 200,000 Goths fleeing the Huns across the Danube — the largest single migration into the empire, and the event that leads directly to Adrianople.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.3–4. Eunapius fragments. Scale and circumstances: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991). Papyrus evidence for administrative processing of refugees.

nodes.label: Battle of Adrianople
nodes.full: The Roman army is annihilated by the Goths; emperor Valens killed — the worst Roman defeat since Cannae and a turning point in late Roman history.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.12–13 (detailed, near-contemporary). Eunapius. Orosius 7.33. Valens's body never found: Ammianus 31.13.15. Date confirmed by multiple sources.

nodes.label: Battle of the Frigidus
nodes.full: Theodosius defeats the pagan usurper Eugenius in a battle later framed as Christianity defeating paganism — a fierce two-day fight decided partly by a windstorm.
nodes.src: Claudian, De III Consulatu Honorii 96–98. Ambrose, De obitu Theodosii 10. Orosius 7.35. The bora windstorm (literary topos or real): Rufinus HE 11.33 records it.

nodes.label: Battle of Argentoratum
nodes.full: Julian (then Caesar under Constantius) defeats the Alamanni king Chnodomar with a much smaller Roman force — his greatest military victory.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 16.12 (detailed). Libanius Oratio 18.56–69. Chnodomar captured and sent to Constantius: Ammianus 16.12.66. Site identified near Strasbourg.

nodes.label: Edict of Toleration (Galerius)
nodes.full: Galerius's deathbed edict ending the Great Persecution and explicitly acknowledging that the campaign to suppress Christianity had failed.
nodes.src: Full Latin text: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 33–34. Greek version: Eusebius HE 8.17. Dated 30 Apr 311 by consular dating in the text itself.

nodes.label: Edict of Milan
nodes.full: Constantine and Licinius agree to full religious toleration and restoration of confiscated Church property — the foundational document of Christian freedom in the West.
nodes.src: Full Latin text: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 48. Greek version: Eusebius HE 10.5. Neither is an 'edict' strictly — a rescript posted at Nicomedia Jun 313.

nodes.label: Foundation of Constantinople
nodes.full: Constantine formally dedicates his new eastern capital on 11 May 330 — a city built from scratch to be the Christian capital of a Christian empire.
nodes.src: Dedication date: Chronicon Paschale s.a. 330. Zosimus 2.30. Jerome Chronicle s.a. 330. Foundation inscription: partially preserved. Extensive numismatic commemoration.

nodes.label: Constantine's Sunday Law
nodes.full: First law mandating rest on Sunday (dies Solis) — bridges pagan solar cult and Christian Sabbath observance in deliberate ambiguity.
nodes.src: Codex Justinianus 3.12.2 (full text). Dated 7 Mar 321 by consular dating. Rordorf, Sunday (1968). The law uses 'dies Solis' (Sun's day), not 'Lord's day'.

nodes.label: Edict of Thessalonica
nodes.full: Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the only legal religion of the empire — all other forms of worship become heresy punishable by law.
nodes.src: Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 (full text survives). Dated by internal consular formula to 27 Feb 380. McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994) for context.

nodes.label: Theodosian edicts banning pagan cult
nodes.full: Theodosius issues a series of edicts closing temples, banning sacrifice and forbidding even entering a temple — effectively outlawing paganism.
nodes.src: CTh 16.10.10 (24 Feb 391) and 16.10.12 (8 Nov 392) — both texts survive in Codex Theodosianus. Zosimus 4.36–37 records the effects with hostility.

nodes.label: Diocletian's army reforms (legacy)
nodes.full: Diocletian's doubling of the army to ~600,000 and introduction of the comitatenses (mobile reserves) vs. limitanei (frontier troops) shapes 4th-century warfare.
nodes.src: John the Lydian, De Mensibus 1.27 records size. Zosimus 2.34 (hostile account). Jones, LRE ch. 17 synthesises papyrus and legal evidence for army structure.

nodes.label: Council of Nicaea I
nodes.full: First ecumenical council, called by Constantine; defines Christ as 'of one substance with the Father' (homoousios) and sets the date of Easter — foundational for all subsequent Christianity.
nodes.src: Acts survive only partially; Eusebius VC 3.6–14 and Athanasius's letters are primary sources. Creed text: Socrates HE 1.8. Date confirmed by multiple chronicles. ~300 bishops attend.

nodes.label: Council of Constantinople I
nodes.full: Confirms Nicene Christianity, extends the creed to include the Holy Spirit, and declares Constantinople second in honour after Rome — the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed still used today.
nodes.src: Acts survive fragmentarily; Gregory of Nazianzus letter 130 is near-contemporary. Creed text in Theoderet HE 5.9. Socrates HE 5.8. 150 bishops; only Eastern bishops invited.

nodes.label: Athanasius vs. Arianism (five exiles)
nodes.full: Athanasius is exiled five times by pro-Arian emperors but never recants — his persistence single-handedly keeps Nicene Christianity alive during Constantius II's reign.
nodes.src: Athanasius's own Apologia contra Arianos (c.357), Historia Arianorum (c.358), and letters document each exile. Exile dates reconstructed by Barnes (1993). 'Athanasius against the world' (Ath. contra mundum) becomes a byword.

nodes.label: Julian's pagan restoration
nodes.full: Julian publicly sacrifices to the old gods, reopens temples, strips the Church of tax privileges and bans Christians from teaching the classics — reversed immediately on his death.
nodes.src: Julian: Orations, Letters, Misopogon (Against the Antiochenes, 362) — all survive. CTh 13.3.5 (Jun 362): bans Christian teachers. Ammianus 22.5 describes sacrifices. Gregory of Nazianzus Orationes 4–5 (hostile).

nodes.label: Altar of Victory controversy
nodes.full: Gratian removes the Altar of Victory from the Senate; Symmachus writes a famous plea for religious tolerance; Ambrose writes the reply forbidding the Christian emperor to comply.
nodes.src: Symmachus Relatio 3 (384): complete text survives. Ambrose Epistulae 17 and 18 (his reply): both survive. Klein (1972). One of the sharpest documented pagan-Christian confrontations.

nodes.label: Arian controversy: Council of Sirmium
nodes.full: The 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' — Constantius II's council tries to resolve the Arian controversy by forbidding use of 'substance' language entirely, causing uproar among both sides.
nodes.src: Text of the Sirmium formula: Athanasius De Synodis 28 (hostile but verbatim). Hilary of Poitiers De Synodis 11 (same formula with commentary). Jerome: 'the whole world groaned and found itself Arian' — Dial. adv. Lucif. 19.

nodes.label: Ulfilas's Gothic Bible translation
nodes.full: Ulfilas invents the Gothic alphabet and translates the Bible into Gothic — the earliest substantial text in any Germanic language and the vehicle for Arian Christianity among the Goths.
nodes.src: Codex Argenteus (Uppsala University Library, DG 1): 188 surviving leaves on purple vellum, 4th–5th c. The only substantial Gothic manuscript. Ulfilas's life: Philostorgius HE 2.5.

nodes.label: Arch of Constantine, Rome
nodes.full: Triumphal arch dedicated to Constantine after the Milvian Bridge victory; combines spolia from Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius with new Constantinian reliefs — a snapshot of artistic transition.
nodes.src: Extant. Dedicatory inscription (CIL VI.1139): 'instinctu divinitatis' — deliberately ambiguous on Christianity. Completed 315 for Constantine's decennalia. L'Orange & von Gerkan (1939).

nodes.label: Old St Peter's Basilica, Rome
nodes.full: Constantine's vast basilica over Peter's tomb — the prototype Christian church building; demolished for the present St Peter's but its foundations survive below.
nodes.src: Liber Pontificalis records construction under Constantine. Foundations excavated 1940–1950 (Vatican Necropolis). Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937–77).

nodes.label: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
nodes.full: Constantine builds over the site of Christ's tomb — the most sacred building in Christianity, dedicated 13 Sep 335, still standing though heavily altered.
nodes.src: Dedication 13 Sep 335: Eusebius VC 3.25–40 (describes construction). Egeria (Peregrinatio, c.381–384) describes the completed building — earliest pilgrim account. Biddle (1999) on archaeology.

nodes.label: Colossal head of Constantine, Rome
nodes.full: Fragment of a 12-metre seated statue of Constantine from the Basilica of Maxentius — the blank, superhuman gaze epitomises the new imperial image.
nodes.src: Capitoline Museums, Rome (Inv. 1072). Marble head 2.6m tall. Part of a seated acrolith (marble head/hands, bronze body). Kleiner (1992), Roman Sculpture.

nodes.label: Hinton St Mary mosaic (Chi-Rho)
nodes.full: The earliest known image of Christ from Britain — a mosaic floor with a Chi-Rho monogram behind a portrait figure, found in a Roman villa in Dorset.
nodes.src: British Museum (1965,0702.1). Found 1963. Dated c.350 by coin evidence. Toynbee (1964), Art in Roman Britain. The identification as Christ (not Constantine) is generally accepted.

nodes.label: Esquiline Treasure (partly)
nodes.full: Hoard of silver plate including the Projecta Casket — aristocratic Christian luxury at its finest, bearing both pagan myth and Christian inscription on the same objects.
nodes.src: British Museum, Bibliothèque nationale Paris. Mango (1994), The Sevso Treasure. Kathleen Shelton, The Esquiline Treasure (1981). Projecta Casket: BM 1866,0520.1.

nodes.label: Palace of Constantinople (Hippodrome complex)
nodes.full: Constantine transforms Byzantium into a vast imperial capital: hippodrome, imperial palace and Christian basilicas built simultaneously on a massive scale.
nodes.src: Hippodrome obelisk inscriptions (extant). Malalas 13.7–8. Eusebius VC 3.48–49. Columns of Serpent (from Delphi), Theodosius, and Constantine still visible in Istanbul.

nodes.label: Christian hymnody — Ambrose of Milan establishes antiphonal singing
nodes.full: Ambrose of Milan introduces antiphonal hymn-singing to the Western Church in 386 during the siege of the basilica by Arian troops — Augustine's Confessions records hearing it for the first time and weeping; the Ambrosian hymns survive as the oldest datable Western Christian music.
nodes.src: Augustine, Confessions 9.7 (c.397): 'It was then first instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung after the manner of the eastern church, to prevent the people from being quite overcome with tedium and sorrow; from that time to this day the practice has been retained.' Four Ambrosian hymns authenticated as genuine: Fontaine (1992), Ambroise de Milan: Hymnes. The 386 date confirmed by Augustine's narrative. Antiphonal singing introduced from Antioch: Ambrose, Epistula 20 to his sister Marcellina.

nodes.label: Eusebius of Caesarea: Ecclesiastical History
nodes.full: The first history of the Christian Church, tracing it from the apostles to Constantine's victory — the founding text of Church historiography, still our primary source for early Christianity.
nodes.src: Multiple editions; final edition c.313. Earliest MS: Codex Sinaiticus (4th c.) contains some portions. Schwartz-Mommsen critical edition (1903–09). Lake translation (1926).

nodes.label: Athanasius: De Incarnatione
nodes.full: Athanasius's foundational theological argument for why God became man — written before the Arian controversy erupted, it becomes the pro-Nicene position's core text.
nodes.src: Complete text survives. Earliest MS: multiple 9th-c. copies. Thomson critical edition (1971). C.S. Lewis's introduction to the Macmillan edition (1946) notes its accessibility.

nodes.label: Ammianus Marcellinus: Res Gestae
nodes.full: The last great Latin historian — a Syrian soldier who continues Tacitus; Books 14–31 survive, covering 353–378, including the Gothic crisis from firsthand experience.
nodes.src: Books 14–31 survive (1–13 lost). Oldest MS: Fuldensis (9th c., Fulda). Author identifies as a soldier: 31.16.9. Seyfarth critical edition (1978). Sabbah (1978) on sources.

nodes.label: Lactantius: Divine Institutes
nodes.full: The first systematic Latin defence of Christianity as a rational philosophy — Lactantius aims to show educated pagans that Christianity is intellectually coherent.
nodes.src: Complete text survives. Earliest MS: 9th c. Brandt-Laubmann critical edition (CSEL 19, 1890). Lactantius was summoned to Trier by Constantine — Jerome, De Viris Ill. 80.

nodes.label: Iamblichus: De Mysteriis
nodes.full: Iamblichus's defence of theurgy (ritual magic as philosophy) — the philosophical foundation for Julian's pagan revival and a major text of Neoplatonism.
nodes.src: Complete text survives. Earliest MS: 12th c. Des Places critical edition (1966). Julian's debt to Iamblichus: Julian Letter to Iamblichus (spurious but revealing), and Eunapius Lives of the Sophists 457–58.

nodes.label: Symmachus: Relatio 3 (Altar of Victory)
nodes.full: Symmachus's elegant plea to Valentinian II to restore the Altar of Victory — the most eloquent surviving defence of Roman paganism and religious pluralism.
nodes.src: Text in Seeck's MGH edition (1883). Ambrose's replies (Ep. 17–18) survive alongside. Klein (1972), Symmachus und die heidnisch-christliche Auseinandersetzung. One of the most studied late-antique texts.

nodes.label: Jerome begins the Vulgate translation
nodes.full: Pope Damasus commissions Jerome to produce a standard Latin Bible — the Vulgate becomes the authoritative text of Western Christianity for over 1,000 years.
nodes.src: Commission by Pope Damasus: Jerome Preface to the Four Gospels (382). Codex Amiatinus (c.692, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence) is the earliest complete copy. Weber-Gryson Stuttgart Vulgate (1969).

nodes.label: Constantinian gold standard (solidus)
nodes.full: Constantine introduces the gold solidus at 72 to the pound — it becomes the most stable currency in the world for over 700 years, surviving as the Byzantine nomisma until 1092.
nodes.src: Numismatic evidence: RIC VII. First minted c.309 at Trier. Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985). Stability confirmed by papyrus price data from Egypt (P.Oxy. various).

nodes.label: Diocletian's tax reform (iugatio-capitatio)
nodes.full: Diocletian's systematic census-based land and head tax — the most ambitious fiscal reorganisation in Roman history, creating uniform assessable tax units (iuga/capita).
nodes.src: Egyptian papyri: P.Cair.Isid. corpus (Karanis village archive, c.296–335). Syrian evidence: inscriptions from Thrace (IGLS). Jones, LRE ch. 13 synthesises the system.

nodes.label: Gothic settlement in Moesia (foederati)
nodes.full: After Adrianople, Theodosius settles the Goths inside the empire as a self-governing federate nation — the first time a barbarian people retain their own laws and leaders on Roman soil.
nodes.src: Treaty date Oct 382: Themistius Oration 16 (delivered to Theodosius). Zosimus 4.34. Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988). Land allocation terms: Jordanes Getica 27 (later source).

nodes.label: Disruption of Eastern trade (Julian's war)
nodes.full: Julian's failed Persian campaign and the cession of Nisibis disrupts the principal eastern trade route; merchants must reroute through Sassanid-controlled territory.
nodes.src: Ephrem the Syrian, Carmina Nisibena (eyewitness to the Roman evacuation). Commercial impact inferred from Procopius's later account of treaty terms (Wars 1.2) and decline of Nisibene trade pottery.

nodes.label: Constantinople's water infrastructure
nodes.full: Constantinople is built with an entirely new water system from scratch: the Aqueduct of Valens (completed 373), cisterns and harbour infrastructure for a city of 500,000.
nodes.src: Aqueduct of Valens: extant (Bozdoğan Kemeri, Istanbul). Completion 373: Socrates HE 4.8. Crow, Bardill & Bayliss, The Water Supply of Byzantine Constantinople (2008).

nodes.label: Constantinian frontier fort programme
nodes.full: Constantine rebuilds and extends the Rhine-Danube frontier with a new generation of forts — bridgeheads on the far side of the rivers as aggressive forward outposts.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 17.1.11 (Julian rebuilds forts, continuing Constantine's work). Johnson, Late Roman Fortifications (1983). Bridgehead forts at Divitia (Cologne), Deutz: excavated.

nodes.label: Gothic alphabet invented (Ulfilas)
nodes.full: Ulfilas creates a new alphabet of 27 letters to transcribe the Gothic language — the first writing system for any Germanic language, invented specifically to translate the Bible.
nodes.src: Philostorgius HE 2.5 records Ulfilas as inventor. Codex Argenteus (Uppsala) preserves the result. The alphabet derives from Greek uncials with some Latin and runic elements: Friedrichsen (1926).

nodes.label: Church basilica building programme
nodes.full: The legalisation of Christianity triggers the first large-scale public building programme in the Christian world — the Roman basilica form adapted and standardised as the church building.
nodes.src: Krautheimer, Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture (1965). Liber Pontificalis records Roman foundations. Eusebius VC 3.29–40 describes the Jerusalem buildings. Engineering continuity from secular basilica documented archaeologically.

nodes.label: Constantine's diplomatic correspondence with Shapur II
nodes.full: Constantine writes to Shapur II presenting himself as protector of Christians in Persia — the first recorded use of religious minority status as a diplomatic instrument; Eusebius preserves the letter, which Shapur II likely read as an interference claim.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Vita Constantini 4.9–13: preserves Constantine's letter to Shapur II in full. The letter's strategic implications: Barnes (1985), Constantine and Eusebius. The Sassanid reaction — intensified Christian persecution under Shapur II — is the documented consequence. A rare case where diplomatic correspondence survives with its response legible in historical events.

nodes.label: Silk Road disruption and the search for alternatives
nodes.full: The cession of Nisibis in 363 — the principal Silk Road hub — forces Rome to reroute eastern trade through the Caucasus and Red Sea; the economic geography of Eurasian trade is visibly restructured by a single military defeat.
nodes.src: Nisibis as trade hub: Lieu (1986), Nisibis as a Centre of the Translation Movement. Ephrem the Syrian's Carmina Nisibena document the Roman evacuation. Post-363 trade rerouting: inferred from the decline of Syrian and rise of Red Sea finds in Western hoards. The economic consequence of the Peace of 363 is underexplored in scholarship: Dignas & Winter (2007).

nodes.label: Translation of Greek texts into Syriac — the bridge tradition
nodes.full: The School of the Persians at Edessa begins the systematic translation of Greek philosophical and medical texts into Syriac — the transmission chain that will eventually carry Aristotle to Baghdad via Syriac; one of the most consequential intellectual relay points in history.
nodes.src: The School at Edessa: Becker (2006), Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom: the School of Nisibis. Vööbus (1965), History of the School of Nisibis. The Syriac translation tradition: Brock (1977), Greek into Syriac and Syriac into Greek, Journal of the Syriac Academy 3. This is the first link in the Greek→Syriac→Arabic translation chain documented by scholars.

nodes.label: Gothic Bible as diplomatic and cultural instrument
nodes.full: Ulfilas's Gothic Bible is simultaneously a religious mission, a cultural transmission event, and a diplomatic act — the Goths gain literacy and Arian Christianity together, creating a cultural bond with Constantinople that shapes their behaviour for a century.
nodes.src: Codex Argenteus (Uppsala, DG 1): 188 leaves of Gothic text. Ulfilas commissioned by the Eastern court: Philostorgius HE 2.5. The diplomatic dimension — Arian Christianity as a connecting identity between Gothic federates and Constantinople — is argued by Heather (1991), Goths and Romans.

nodes.label: Sassanid Empire under Shapur II
nodes.full: Shapur II's 70-year reign makes Persia Rome's most dangerous and consistent rival; he besieges Nisibis three times, recaptures it in 363 and kills the emperor Julian.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus (multiple books) is the main Roman source. Tabari's Chronicle (9th c.) for Persian perspective. Shapur II's rock inscriptions at Taq-e Bostan (extant).

nodes.label: Hunnic expansion westward
nodes.full: The Huns appear on the Pontic steppe around 370 and push the Goths westward with devastating speed — the chain reaction that produces the Gothic crossing of 376 and Adrianople.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.2–3 (describes Hunnic way of life). Eunapius fragments. Physical evidence: Hunnic cauldron finds cluster west of Don river. Heather, Goths and Romans (1991) ch. 3.

nodes.label: Division of empire at Theodosius's death
nodes.full: Theodosius dies leaving the empire to his two sons — 11-year-old Honorius in the West and 18-year-old Arcadius in the East — a division that proves permanent.
nodes.src: Death 17 Jan 395: Zosimus 4.59; Claudian, De III Consulatu Honorii. Stilicho's guardianship: Claudian, De Consulatu Stilichonis. Orosius 7.36 for the political consequences.

nodes.label: Ammianus on climate and natural disasters
nodes.full: Ammianus Marcellinus records major earthquakes (365 AD tsunami devastating Alexandria), floods and crop failures — unusually rich environmental documentation for the period.
nodes.src: Earthquake and tsunami 21 Jul 365: Ammianus 26.10 (eyewitness account of waves reaching Egypt). Kelly Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017) ch. 6. Archaeological evidence: destruction layers at coastal sites.

nodes.label: Constantius II criminalises passive same-sex acts
nodes.full: The first Roman imperial law explicitly criminalising same-sex acts: Codex Theodosianus 9.7.3 threatens punishment by the sword for the passive role — marking a shift from the Lex Scantinia's social stigma to criminal law, driven by Christian influence on the court.
nodes.src: CTh 9.7.3 (342 CE): text survives in the Codex Theodosianus. Boswell (1980) pp.120–123. The law's Christian theological background: Constantius II's Arian Christianity shapes the legislation. Williams (2010), Roman Homosexuality, ch.8: the shift from status-based to act-based criminal law. This is the first dateable legislative CATEGORICAL SHIFT in Roman law on this subject.

nodes.label: Theodosian Code 9.7.6 — burning alive prescribed
nodes.full: Valentinian II prescribes death by burning for men who take the passive role in same-sex acts — escalating from the sword (342) to burning, and removing the citizen/non-citizen distinction entirely; a major step in the Christianisation of Roman criminal law.
nodes.src: CTh 9.7.6 (390 CE): full text survives in the Codex Theodosianus. Boswell (1980) pp.123–124. The burning penalty: parallels Mosaic law (Lev 20:13 Septuagint) — the first direct Biblical legal borrowing in Roman statute. The progression from 342 to 390 is the key arc of 4th-century legal history on this subject.

nodes.label: Perpetua's Passio — a woman's first-person prison account
nodes.full: The Passio Sanctarum Perpetuae et Felicitatis contains sections written by Perpetua herself in prison — one of the only surviving first-person texts by a woman from antiquity; she describes a dream in which she becomes a man to fight in the arena.
nodes.src: Passio Perpetuae et Felicitatis: Latin text, oldest MS 11th c. but content dated 203 CE by internal evidence. Perpetua's own sections: 3.1–10.13. The gender-transformation dream: 10.7 ('I became a man'). Scholarly debate on authenticity: Shaw (1993), JRS. Gold (2018), Perpetua: Athlete of God. Widely circulated in North Africa by the 4th century.

nodes.label: Gallae — priests of Cybele and gender variance at Rome
nodes.full: The Gallae, castrated priests of Cybele, occupy a recognised gender-variant role in Roman religious life — wearing women's dress, using feminine pronouns, begging in public; their existence is extensively documented before the cult's suppression in 391.
nodes.src: Multiple sources: Lucian De Dea Syria; Catullus 63; Augustine De Civitate Dei 7.26 (hostile but detailed). Archaeological: Palatine sanctuary of Cybele excavated. The Gallae as recognised gender-variant category: Roller (1999), In Search of God the Mother. Suppression under Theodosius 391: CTh 16.10.10. This is BOTH evidence of the practice AND a categorical shift when the cult is banned.

nodes.label: Macrina the Elder — Gregory of Nyssa's theological biography
nodes.full: Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina documents his sister's decision to remain unmarried, manage a monastic community, and engage in theological debate — the most detailed 4th-century account of a woman exercising intellectual and spiritual authority outside marriage.
nodes.src: Gregory of Nyssa, Vita Macrinae (c.382): Greek text survives complete. Callahan translation (1967). Macrina's philosophical dialogue On the Soul and Resurrection (Gregory attributes it to her): survives. Hart (2019) on Macrina's intellectual independence. The text is unusual in presenting a woman as the theological teacher of her male relatives.

edges: Diocletian's doubled army and the comitatenses/limitanei split are the system he abdicates from
the Constantinian forward-fort programme continues Diocletian's frontier reorganisation
Galerius becomes eastern Augustus on Diocletian's abdication
Galerius issues the deathbed Edict of Toleration, ending the Great Persecution and admitting it had failed
Maxentius seizes Rome against the Tetrarchic succession that Diocletian's retirement left unstable
Constantine defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge
the Arch of Constantine commemorates it, with 'instinctu divinitatis' deliberately ambiguous
the colossal 12-metre acrolith from the Basilica of Maxentius carries the new superhuman imperial image
Constantine makes Licinius his eastern colleague and brother-in-law
toleration becomes full legal freedom and restoration of confiscated Church property
Constantine and Licinius agree the Edict of Milan
the joint rescript is posted at Nicomedia in Licinius's east
Constantine defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis to become sole emperor
Constantine founds Constantinople as a Christian capital built from scratch
hippodrome, palace and basilicas raised simultaneously on a massive scale
an entirely new water system — the Aqueduct of Valens, cisterns — for a city of half a million
Constantine's Sunday Law mandates rest on the 'dies Solis', bridging solar cult and Christian observance
Constantine convenes the Council of Nicaea and presides over it
Eusebius, present at Nicaea, is the primary source for it
Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History traces the Church from the apostles to Constantine's victory
Constantine builds Old St Peter's over the apostle's tomb
and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre over the site of Christ's tomb
legalisation triggers the first large-scale Christian public building programme
the Roman basilica form adapted and standardised as the church building
the Jerusalem complex is part of the same programme
Constantine introduces the gold solidus — the most stable currency in the world for 700 years
Lactantius, summoned to Trier as tutor to Constantine's son, writes the first systematic Latin defence of Christianity
Constantine writes to Shapur II presenting himself as protector of Persia's Christians
Shapur II reads it as an interference claim; intensified persecution of Persian Christians follows
Athanasius's De Incarnatione, written before the controversy, becomes the pro-Nicene position's core text
Nicaea's 'homoousios' is the formula Athanasius spends his life defending
the Arian Constantius II exiles Athanasius five times, and he never recants
Constantius's Council of Sirmium tries to ban 'substance' language altogether — 'the whole world groaned and found itself Arian'
Athanasius's persistence keeps Nicene Christianity alive until the Council of Constantinople confirms it in 381
Theodosius convenes the council that fixes the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed
Gregory of Nyssa, whose Life of Macrina presents his sister as his theological teacher, is one of the Cappadocians shaping the council
Ulfilas invents a 27-letter alphabet specifically to translate the Bible into Gothic
the Gothic Bible is a religious mission, a cultural transmission and a diplomatic act at once
the Eastern Arian court commissions and shelters Ulfilas
Ulfilas's Gothic church is Arian — the confession the Eastern court then held
Arian Christianity becomes a connecting identity between the Gothic federates and Constantinople
Constantius II raises his cousin Julian to Caesar, then Julian is acclaimed Augustus by his troops
Julian's crushing victory over the Alamanni at Strasbourg makes his military reputation
Julian publicly sacrifices to the old gods, reopens temples and bans Christians from teaching the classics
Iamblichus's defence of theurgy is the philosophical foundation of Julian's revival
Julian launches a massive invasion of Persia
Shapur II's Persia is the target — and Julian reaches Ctesiphon but cannot take it
the army elects the Christian general Jovian on the spot
the pagan restoration is reversed the moment Julian dies
the disaster forces the Peace of 363 — Nisibis and fifteen towns ceded to Persia
Jovian concludes the humiliating peace, then dies within eight months
the cession of Nisibis disrupts the principal eastern trade route
the Silk Road reroutes through the Caucasus and Red Sea — economic geography restructured by one defeat
with Nisibis lost, the Syriac translation of Greek learning concentrates at the School of the Persians in Edessa
the army picks Valentinian, who names his brother Valens co-emperor for the east
Valentinian I spends his reign fortifying the Rhine frontier
Valentinian's son Gratian succeeds him in the west
the Huns push the Goths westward with devastating speed — the chain reaction behind the crossing of 376
Valens admits some 200,000 Goths across the Danube
the botched settlement leads directly to Adrianople two years later
the Roman army is annihilated and Valens is killed — his body never found
the catastrophe brings Theodosius to the eastern throne
after Adrianople, Theodosius settles the Goths as a self-governing federate nation on Roman soil
the first time a barbarian people keep their own laws and leaders inside the empire
Ammianus Marcellinus, a soldier, writes the near-contemporary account of the Gothic crisis
and the detailed eyewitness narrative of Julian's Persian campaign
and the first Roman description of the Huns
Ammianus is also the eyewitness for the 365 tsunami that devastated Alexandria
Gratian removes the Altar of Victory from the Senate and strips the pagan priests' stipends
Symmachus's Relatio 3 is the eloquent plea to restore it
Ambrose, who writes the reply forbidding the emperor to comply, is the same bishop who introduces antiphonal hymnody at Milan
Ambrose introduces the hymns during the siege of his basilica by the Arian court — the Nicene-Arian struggle still live in the west
Gratian is murdered in a military revolt; Theodosius becomes the dominant emperor
the Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the only legal religion — all else is heresy
and the 391–392 edicts close the temples, ban sacrifice, and forbid even entering a temple
Julian's failed top-down revival had shown paganism could not be restored — a generation later it is simply outlawed
the cult of Cybele is suppressed in 391, ending the recognised gender-variant role of its Gallae
Theodosius defeats the pagan usurper Eugenius at the Frigidus
the battle is framed as Christianity defeating paganism
Theodosius dies in 395 leaving the empire to his two young sons — a division that proves permanent
Constantius II issues the first Roman law explicitly criminalising the passive role in same-sex acts, punishable by the sword
the penalty escalates from the sword (342) to burning alive (390), the citizen distinction dropped
the burning penalty borrows directly from the Septuagint — the Christianisation of Roman criminal law
Constantius's Arian Christianity is the theological background to the legislation
Pope Damasus commissions Jerome's Vulgate the same decade Nicene Christianity becomes law
Perpetua's prison diary and the Life of Macrina are among the very few late-antique texts foregrounding a woman's own voice
the Passio circulates widely in North Africa as Christian literature consolidates
Diocletian's census-based land-and-head tax is the fiscal base the stable solidus then sits on top of
the tax reform and the army expansion are two halves of the same Diocletianic reorganisation
the Chi-Rho mosaic in a Dorset villa shows the new religion reaching the empire's furthest province
the Esquiline Treasure's silver carries pagan myth and Christian inscription on the same objects — an aristocracy mid-conversion
